Maladaptive Strategies.value: I put on loud music or TV
constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette: Thomas stood in the dim corridor of his second-floor apartment, the heavy deadbolt thrown across the door, listening to the distant hum of the city. Decades earlier, while overseeing a major renovation at the historic Meridian Hotel, a corroded pressure valve had burst, flooding the service tunnels with a thick, acrid cloud of industrial solvents. He had tried to clear the air, but the fumes had seared his lungs and left him coughing violently against a damp brick wall. In the months that followed, what began as a panic attack over a minor plumbing leak solidified into a relentless state of hyperarousal. The smell of paint thinner now hit him without warning, dragging the full, suffocating terror of that tunnel back to him, even though his mind refused to compile the memory into a coherent picture. Those fragmented pieces of the event—just a glare of emergency lights and the metallic taste of fear—would surface randomly, and when those disjointed fragments appeared, the unexplained emotional surge confirmed his growing belief that he could no longer trust his own body. His daily rounds through the hotel’s service corridors became a gauntlet of triggers; when the freight elevator jolted violently on the fourth floor, Thomas’s heart hammered against his ribs and he immediately retreated to the linen closet, convinced the structural supports were failing. His conviction that his body was fundamentally unreliable and that he was entirely helpless to stop bad things from happening directly amplified his sense of immediate peril, cementing his daily reality that he was only truly safe within a two-room perimeter of his apartment. Every unexpected noise in the hallway was treated as a breach of that boundary. As his nervous system remained locked in high alert, the olfactory flashes grew more intrusive, fracturing his remaining composure into isolated shards of panic that refused to connect. When those sudden sensory recollections of burning solvents surfaced, they instantly triggered his nervous system to register danger, ensuring the memory remained a threat rather than a recollection. He knew he could not stop the disaster from repeating itself, so he stopped managing the property floor and instead focused entirely on fortifying his walls. To keep the panic at bay, Thomas turned to sensory overload, cranking the volume on the television or blasting classical music until the walls vibrated, while simultaneously scanning his own mind for any whisper of madness. His unrelenting sense of danger pushed him toward this constant auditory noise, and when the scent of industrial solvent lingered in his memory, the rising dread compelled him to turn up the radio and step further from the window. His constant avoidance of the old renovation site meant he never processed what had actually happened, leaving his fear of sounds and enclosed spaces unchallenged. Each time he reached for the remote or checked the locks, the temporary relief only confirmed his growing conviction that he could never rely on his own mind or body again. Now seventy-six and divorced, Thomas finally scheduled an appointment after a sudden steam vent near his building’s entrance triggered a full physiological collapse, leaving him unable to walk. He sat in the waiting room, his hands clenched around a paper cup of water, terrified that the walls would close in or that his heart would simply stop. What brought him through the door was not a desire to feel better, but a desperate need to understand why his own body continued to wage war against him long after the solvents had vanished. He hoped, more than anything, that someone might finally help him separate the past from the present, before the silence in his apartment became louder than the noise he used to drown it out.
